title: US Inflation Cools to 3.4% in July but Wages Still Trail Rising Prices
excerpt: Gas and grocery costs eased for the second month running, yet the gap between pay growth and price increases continues to erode household purchasing power.
body:
• Annual CPI inflation fell to 3.4% in July from 3.5% in June, with monthly prices rising just 0.1%
  • Gas prices dropped 2.9% and grocery costs edged down 0.1%, offering some relief at the pump and checkout
  • Wages grew just 3.2%, trailing the 3.4% inflation rate, meaning real purchasing power continues to shrink
  • Home prices are growing just 1.2% in 2026, effectively declining in real terms, while mortgage rates hold near 6.3%

Inflation Ticks Down, but Not Enough

Annual inflation slowed for the second consecutive month in July, falling to 3.4% from 3.5% in June, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Prices rose just 0.1% on a monthly basis, in line with economists' expectations and a modest rebound from June's 0.4% decline — the first monthly drop in six years.

https://x.com/PeterSchiff/status/2088248419949084788

The improvement was driven largely by falling gas prices, which dropped 2.9% in July after a 9.7% plunge in June. Grocery costs also edged down 0.1%, running at an annual rate of 2.7%. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy, rose 0.2% monthly and 2.5% annually — matching a nearly five-year low first reached earlier this year.

"The economy isn't out of the woods from the threat that inflation poses for everyday Americans, but price pressures aren't hot to the touch either."

— Christopher Rupkey, Chief Economist, FwdBonds

The Wage Gap Widens the Squeeze

Even with cooling headline numbers, the data offers little comfort to many households. Wage growth stood at 3.2% in July — below the 3.4% inflation rate — meaning workers' real purchasing power continued to erode. After five years of elevated prices, the cumulative cost-of-living burden remains heavy.

Retailers and grocery chains have been rolling back some prices this summer, but economists warn that relief may be short-lived. "There was a major effort by big-box discounters and grocery chains to roll back some of their prices," Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, told CNN. "The problem is, the upward pressure on prices once the fertilizer and energy costs start to filter in as we get into the fall harvest."

Services-sector inflation, including medical care, airfares and car repairs, also continues to run hot, keeping underlying price pressures alive even as goods prices moderate.

Housing: Cheaper in Real Terms, Still Expensive

Shelter costs, which account for roughly a third of the CPI basket, rose just 0.1% in July. Hotel and motel prices fell 3.3%, likely linked to the end of the FIFA World Cup, though owners' equivalent rent — a proxy for homeownership costs — still climbed 0.3%.

For prospective homebuyers, the picture is mixed. Home prices are on track to grow just 1.2% in 2026, according to Realtor.com's midyear forecast — trailing projected inflation of 3.4%, which means home values are effectively declining in real terms. Monthly mortgage payments for a typical buyer are projected to be 1.9% below last year's.

But mortgage rates remain stubbornly elevated at around 6.3%, with market expectations shifting from rate cuts to one or two possible hikes by December following the Middle East conflict.

The Fed's Next Move

The cooler inflation data pushed odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in September down to roughly 38%, according to CME FedWatch, from 48% a day earlier. The Fed currently holds its benchmark rate at 3.50%-3.75%.

"In-line inflation will keep the 'no need to hike rates' narrative that took hold after last week's jobs report intact."

— Ellen Zentner, Chief Economic Strategist, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management

But policymakers will still receive August's employment and inflation data before their September meeting, and economists expect the pace of price increases to pick up again as rising oil prices filter through the economy. Energy costs have been especially volatile since the Middle East war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, adding uncertainty to an already cautious Fed.

For households budgeting through another year of above-target inflation, the July numbers mark a step in the right direction — but not yet the finish line.
